newsitem.title: USA: Psychic Jeane Dixon dead at 79.
newsitem.headline: Psychic Jeane Dixon dead at 79.

text.p: Noted psychic and astrologer Jeane Dixon died of a heart attack at Sibley Hospital in Washington on Saturday afternoon, a spokeswoman for the hospital said.

Nursing coordinator Joan Vincent said Dixon died shortly after her arrival at the hospital. The woman whose name became virtually synonomous with the term "psychic" celebrated her 79th birthday on Jan. 5.
Dixon, whose daily "Horoscope and Predictions" column was read by millions, was also the president of a realty company together with her husband, James Dixon.
An adviser to many famous clients, including Nancy Reagan, Dixon rose to national prominence for her prediction that President John Kennedy would die in office.
More recently, however, she predicted that a descendant of Egyptian Queen Nefertiti would come to power, uniting the world.
Reagan, after deciding Dixon had lost her powers, later shifted her allegiance to rival astrologer Joan Quigley.

The author of at least seven books, including an astrological cookbook and a horoscope book for dogs, Dixon was a leading exponent of extrasensory perception, as well as an influential Washington socialite.
"Our lives are programmed at conception and are endowed with purpose and meaning," she once wrote.
She was close friends with Sen. Strom Thurmond, the South Carolina Republican, for over 30 years and became the godmother to his son, Paul Thurmond.

Dixon wrote a daily horoscope column giving people advice on everything from finances to their love lives, and at the start of each year she released a long list of predictions, which supermarket tabloids loved to publish and then double-check.

For 1997, Dixon predicted that actor Alec Baldwin would become terribly ill, comedian Ellen DeGeneres would have a run-in with the Secret Service when she crashed the presidential inauguration; a plane would crash in late October, and there would be an outbreak of illness among the animals on Michael Jackson's ranch.
For millions of Americans, Dixon's name was a household word, one that symbolised more than her life's work, but the whole genre of psychic predictions.
